Plural form: vertices (though "vertexes" is also accepted)

A vertex is always a precise, singular point — never a region, never a stretch of space, but always one exact location. Depending on the context, it is the point where things converge (come together), where something reaches its highest or lowest extreme, or where a curve changes direction. This single idea — a specific, defining point — is the thread connecting every use of this word across every field.
In Everyday Language

In general, non-technical usage, vertex simply means the highest point or tip of something. The peak of a mountain, the pointed top of a cone, the very tip of a pyramid — any of these can be called a vertex. In this sense, it is a formal, precise synonym for "apex" or "peak." Most people, however, encounter vertex far more often in its technical meanings, particularly in geometry.
In Geometry: Angles

When two rays — think of them as two straight lines that each start at the same point and shoot outward — come together, they form an angle. The exact point where those two rays meet and originate is called the vertex of that angle. Put simply, it is the corner of the angle. If you hold two pens so they touch at one end and splay outward like the letter V, the spot where they touch is the vertex. The angle's arms spread away from it, but the vertex itself is that one fixed point.
In Geometry: Flat Shapes (Polygons)

A polygon is any flat, closed shape made entirely of straight sides — triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons, and so on. Every corner of a polygon is a vertex. A triangle has three sides meeting at three corners, so it has three vertices. A square has four corners, giving it four vertices. A pentagon has five corners and five vertices. The pattern holds for any polygon: the number of vertices equals the number of sides. Each vertex is the precise point where two sides of the shape meet.
In Geometry: 3D Shapes (Polyhedra)

The same idea extends naturally into three dimensions. A polyhedron is a solid shape whose surfaces are all flat faces — a cube, a pyramid, a prism, and so on. Any sharp corner of such a 3D shape, where edges come together, is a vertex. A cube has eight vertices, one at each of its eight corners. A square pyramid has five vertices: four at the base corners and one at the pointed tip at the top. Wherever edges converge at a point in a 3D solid, that point is a vertex.
In Geometry: Parabolas

A parabola is a smooth, symmetrical, U-shaped curve (or an upside-down U). It has exactly one special turning point — the very bottom of the U (if it opens upward) or the very top (if it opens downward). This turning point is called the vertex of the parabola. It is where the curve stops descending and starts rising, or vice versa. It is also the point where the parabola is closest to its axis of symmetry. For example, the simple curve described by y = x² has its vertex at the origin (0, 0), the lowest point of the U shape. The vertex of a parabola is significant because it represents the minimum or maximum value of the curve.
In Graph Theory

In mathematics, a "graph" does not always mean a bar chart or a line plot. In graph theory, a graph is a structure made up of points connected by lines. Each individual point in such a structure is called a vertex, and the lines connecting vertices are called edges. Think of a train network: each station is a vertex, and each rail line between two stations is an edge. This usage is extremely important in computer science, network analysis, social science, and logistics, because graph theory is used to model anything that involves connections between things — from computer networks to social relationships to road maps.
In Anatomy

In human anatomy, the vertex is the very top of the skull — the crown of the head. It is the highest point of the cranium when a person is standing upright. Doctors, surgeons, and anatomists use this term with great precision. It is especially important in obstetrics (the medical field dealing with childbirth): when a baby is born head-first with the crown of the head leading the way, this is called a "vertex presentation," and it is the most common and safest position for birth.
In Astronomy

Astronomers use vertex (also called the solar apex) to describe the point in the sky toward which the Sun — along with the entire solar system — appears to be traveling as it moves through the Milky Way galaxy. Since our solar system is in constant motion relative to neighboring stars, the direction it is headed can be mapped onto the sky, and that destination point is the vertex. The word is also occasionally used in astronomy to mean the zenith — the point in the sky directly overhead any given observer.
In Particle Physics

In particle physics, a vertex refers to the precise point in space where subatomic particles interact, collide, or decay. When scientists study particle collisions in accelerators like CERN's Large Hadron Collider, they reconstruct the vertices — the exact points where the interactions occurred — to determine what particles were produced, destroyed, or transformed. Identifying vertices accurately is essential to understanding the results of experiments.
The Unifying Thread

Across every field, "vertex" always names the same kind of thing: one exact, special, indivisible point. It is never approximate or spread out. Whether it is the corner where two sides of a triangle meet, the tip of a pyramid, the turning point of a parabola, a node in a network, the crown of a human skull, or a point of particle collision — vertex is always the name for that one defining location which holds the most geometric or structural significance in its context. Mastering this core idea — that a vertex is always a precise, meaningful point — will allow you to understand the word correctly no matter where you encounter it.
